column1: 21:1|Jehoshaphat rested with his ancestors and was buried beside them in the City of David. His son Jehoram succeeded him as king.|Keeps rest/burial distinct and names the succeeding son clearly.

21:2|Jehoram's brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat, were Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariahu, Michael, and Shephatiah. All were sons of Jehoshaphat king of Israel.|Retains both similar Azariah names and the source's title Israel.

21:3|Their father gave them generous gifts of silver, gold, and precious things, along with fortified cities in Judah. But he gave the kingdom to Jehoram because he was the firstborn.|Distinguishes gifts and cities from the firstborn's royal inheritance.

21:4|Once Jehoram had taken over his father's kingdom and secured his power, he killed all his brothers with the sword, along with some of Israel's officials.|Makes consolidation and fratricide explicit without excusing the violence.
21:5|Jehoram was thirty-two when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for eight years.|Preserves accession age and reign length for the repeated closing notice.

21:6|He followed the ways of Israel's kings, as Ahab's house had done, for he had married Ahab's daughter. He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes.|Connects marriage and dynasty while retaining the narrator's moral assessment.

21:7|Yet the LORD was unwilling to destroy David's house because of the covenant he had made with David. He had promised to give a lamp to David and his sons for all time.|Preserves the covenant and lamp image rather than reducing them to succession.
21:8|During Jehoram's reign, Edom broke free from Judah's rule and set up a king of its own.|Renders under Judah's hand as political rule, with Edom's agency intact.

21:9|Jehoram crossed over with his commanders and all his chariots. Rising during the night, he struck the Edomites who had surrounded him and the chariot commanders.|Retains difficult final object without inserting an escape or victory claim.

21:10|Edom has remained in revolt against Judah to this day. Libnah also revolted against Jehoram's rule at that time, because he had abandoned the LORD, the God of his ancestors.|Keeps the narrator's time perspective and stated reason for Libnah's revolt.

21:11|He also built high places in Judah's hills, led Jerusalem's inhabitants into prostitution, and drove Judah astray.|Retains prostitution as the source's sharp religious image, explained in vocabulary.

21:12|A letter came to him from Elijah the prophet: “This is what the LORD, the God of your ancestor David, says: You have not followed the ways of your father Jehoshaphat or of Asa king of Judah.|Preserves Elijah's letter and the two named standards without chronology repair.

21:13|Instead, you have followed the ways of Israel's kings and led Judah and Jerusalem's inhabitants into prostitution, just as Ahab's house did. You have also killed your brothers, members of your father's house who were better than you.|Keeps divine accusation, religious metaphor, and explicit comparison with murdered brothers.

21:14|So the LORD is about to strike your people, your sons, your wives, and everything you own with a devastating blow.|Preserves all affected groups and property without reducing harm to Jehoram alone.

21:15|You yourself will suffer terribly from a disease in your bowels, until, as the illness goes on day after day, your bowels come out.”|Retains bodily horror and duration rather than euphemizing the judgment.

21:16|The LORD stirred up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines and of the Arabs who lived beside the Cushites.|Preserves divine agency and geographical relationship without modern ethnic substitution.

21:17|They invaded Judah, broke into it, and carried off everything they found in the king's palace, as well as his sons and wives. No son was left to him except Jehoahaz, his youngest.|Retains Jehoahaz here and the captivity language without importing later deaths.
21:18|After all this, the LORD struck him with an incurable disease in his bowels.|Keeps the source's attribution and incurability explicit.

21:19|Time passed. At the end of two years, his bowels came out because of his illness, and he died in terrible pain. His people made no funeral burning for him as they had for his ancestors.|Retains two years and distinguishes funeral burning from cremation.

21:20|He was thirty-two when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for eight years. He departed with no one longing for him. They buried him in the City of David, but not in the royal tombs.|Repeats source figures and preserves the stark unregretted departure and burial exclusion.

22:1|Jerusalem's inhabitants made his youngest son Ahaziah king in his place, because the raiding band that came into the camp with the Arabs had killed all the older sons. So Ahaziah son of Jehoram became king of Judah.|Keeps older sons' deaths here and identifies the new king despite name variation.

22:2|Ahaziah was forty-two when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for one year. His mother's name was Athaliah, a daughter of Omri.|Retains pinned forty-two despite chronological difficulty; daughter remains broad kinship wording.
22:3|He too followed the ways of Ahab's house, for his mother counseled him to do wrong.|Keeps maternal counsel as the narrator's explanation, not a generalized claim.

22:4|He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, just as Ahab's house had done. After his father's death, they became his advisers, bringing about his ruin.|Makes plural advisers and the ruinous consequence clear.

22:5|Following their advice, he joined Jehoram son of Ahab, king of Israel, in a war against Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth-gilead. The Arameans wounded Joram.|Retains Jehoram/Joram variation with a short identifying note.

22:6|He returned to Jezreel to recover from the wounds they had given him at Ramah when he fought Hazael king of Aram. Azariah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, went down to Jezreel to see Jehoram son of Ahab because he was wounded.|Preserves Azariah as written here rather than silently replacing it with Ahaziah.

22:7|God brought about Ahaziah's downfall through his visit to Joram. When he arrived, he went out with Jehoram to meet Jehu son of Nimshi, whom the LORD had anointed to cut off Ahab's house.|Retains God's role and son of Nimshi without harmonizing genealogy.

22:8|As Jehu was executing judgment on Ahab's house, he found Judah's officials and the sons of Ahaziah's brothers who attended Ahaziah, and he killed them.|Distinguishes nephews from brothers and retains the judgment framing.

22:9|He searched for Ahaziah, and they captured him hiding in Samaria. They brought him to Jehu and put him to death. They buried him, saying, “He was a descendant of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart.” No one in Ahaziah's house had the strength to hold the kingdom.|Makes multi-generation son intelligible; preserves capture location and absence of a strong successor.

22:10|When Athaliah, Ahaziah's mother, saw that her son was dead, she rose up and destroyed all the royal offspring of Judah's house.|Retains the sweeping slaughter report, with the rescued exception in the following verse.

22:11|But Jehoshabeath, the king's daughter, took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king's sons who were being killed. She put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Jehoshabeath was King Jehoram's daughter, the wife of Jehoiada the priest, and Ahaziah's sister. She hid Joash from Athaliah so that Athaliah did not kill him.|Unfolds dense kinship and pronouns while preserving the woman's decisive rescue.
22:12|He remained hidden with them in God's house for six years, while Athaliah ruled the land.|Retains six years and simultaneous rule without relocating the hiding place.

23:1|In the seventh year, Jehoiada took courage and brought the commanders of hundreds into a covenant with him: Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zichri.|Keeps all five commanders and fathers, and retains covenant language.

23:2|They traveled through Judah and gathered the Levites from all its cities, along with Israel's ancestral family heads. They came to Jerusalem.|Distinguishes Levites and family heads without narrowing Israel to Judah.

23:3|The whole assembly made a covenant with the king in God's house. Jehoiada told them, “Here is the king's son! He will reign, as the LORD promised concerning David's sons.|Names the speaker supplied by context and keeps the Davidic promise.
23:4|This is what you must do: a third of you priests and Levites coming on duty on the Sabbath must guard the thresholds,|Makes the Sabbath shift and first third's task readable across verse labels.
23:5|a third must be at the palace, and a third at the Foundation Gate. All the people must be in the courts of the LORD's house.|Preserves the other two stations and the people's separate place.

23:6|No one may enter the LORD's house except the priests and the Levites serving there. They may enter because they are holy; all the people must keep the LORD's requirements.|Keeps restricted sacred access and holiness without equating it with moral superiority.

23:7|The Levites must surround the king, each with his weapon in hand. Anyone who enters the house must be put to death. Stay with the king wherever he comes and goes.”|Retains death penalty and comprehensive protection, with context defining intrusion.

23:8|The Levites and all Judah did everything Jehoiada the priest commanded. Each commander took his men, both those coming on duty on the Sabbath and those going off, for Jehoiada the priest had not dismissed the divisions.|Explains why both shifts remain without importing the Kings account's personnel.

23:9|Jehoiada the priest gave the commanders of hundreds the spears, large shields, and small shields that had belonged to King David and were in God's house.|Retains three weapon categories and their Davidic provenance.

23:10|He stationed all the people, each with his weapon in hand, from the south side of the house to the north side, by the altar and the house, surrounding the king.|Renders right/left spatially for an east-facing sanctuary, retaining altar and king.

23:11|They brought out the king's son, put the crown on him, gave him the testimony, and made him king. Jehoiada and his sons anointed him and cried, “Long live the king!”|Retains uncertain testimony as a biblical term with a selective note.
23:12|Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and praising the king. She went to the people at the LORD's house.|Keeps running and praise rather than substituting a generic celebration.

23:13|There she saw the king standing by his pillar at the entrance, with the commanders and trumpeters beside him. All the people of the land were rejoicing and sounding trumpets, while the singers played their instruments and led the praise. Athaliah tore her clothes and shouted, “Treason! Treason!”|Preserves the public scene, pillar ambiguity, and repeated accusation.

23:14|Jehoiada the priest brought out the commanders of hundreds who were in charge of the army and told them, “Take her out between the ranks. Anyone who follows her must be killed with the sword.” For the priest had said, “Do not kill her in the LORD's house.”|Keeps both lethal orders and the sacred-location restriction in distinct speech.
23:15|They seized her, and she came to the entrance of the Horse Gate at the palace. There they put her to death.|Preserves seizure, route, and execution without adding a trial.
23:16|Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, all the people, and the king, that they would be the LORD's people.|Retains himself as the first party rather than harmonizing to the LORD.

23:17|All the people went to Baal's house and tore it down. They smashed its altars and images and killed Mattan, Baal's priest, in front of the altars.|Makes destruction and killing explicit, preserving Mattan's identity.

23:18|Jehoiada placed the oversight of the LORD's house in the hands of the Levitical priests whom David had assigned to it. They were to offer burnt offerings to the LORD as written in Moses' law, with rejoicing and song according to David's directions.|Follows linked priests/Levites wording while noting another possible coordination.
23:19|He stationed gatekeepers at the gates of the LORD's house so that no one unclean in any respect could enter.|Retains comprehensive ritual uncleanness rather than substituting moral worthiness.

23:20|He took the commanders of hundreds, the nobles, the people's rulers, and all the people of the land, and brought the king down from the LORD's house. They entered the palace through the Upper Gate and seated the king on the royal throne.|Keeps four participant groups and the procession's descent and destination.
23:21|All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet. Athaliah had been put to death with the sword.|Preserves both communal response and the violent basis of the quiet.
24:1|Joash was seven when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for forty years. His mother's name was Zibiah, from Beer-sheba.|Retains childhood accession, forty-year reign, and maternal origin.
24:2|Joash did what was right in the LORD's eyes throughout the lifetime of Jehoiada the priest.|Keeps the lifetime qualification that structures the following reversal.
24:3|Jehoiada obtained two wives for him, and Joash had sons and daughters.|Clarifies the likely referent of him without hiding the two marriages.
24:4|Some time later, Joash set his heart on restoring the LORD's house.|Retains heart language as purposeful intention, with source segmentation unchanged in binding.

24:5|He gathered the priests and Levites and told them, “Go out to Judah's cities and collect money from all Israel every year to repair your God's house. See to it quickly.” But the Levites did not act quickly.|Preserves annual collection and the pointed repetition of quickly.

24:6|The king summoned Jehoiada the chief priest and asked, “Why have you not required the Levites to bring in from Judah and Jerusalem the levy of Moses, the LORD's servant, and Israel's assembly for the tent of the testimony?”|Retains the levy and tent connection without inventing a new tax amount.

24:7|For the sons of that wicked woman Athaliah had broken into God's house and even used all the sacred things from the LORD's house for the Baals.|Keeps sons as agents and the narrator's description of Athaliah.
24:8|At the king's command, they made a chest and placed it outside the gate of the LORD's house.|Distinguishes collection chest from covenant ark by context.

24:9|They issued a proclamation in Judah and Jerusalem to bring to the LORD the levy that Moses, God's servant, had imposed on Israel in the wilderness.|Preserves Mosaic wilderness connection and the offering's recipient.

24:10|All the officials and all the people were glad to bring their contributions and drop them into the chest until they had finished.|Leaves finished without supplying a particular collection target or deadline.

24:11|Whenever the chest was brought by the Levites to the king's officers and they saw that it held a large sum, the king's scribe and the chief priest's officer came and emptied it. They carried it back to its place. They did this day after day and collected a great deal of money.|Unfolds collection procedure and joint oversight without omitting repetition.

24:12|The king and Jehoiada gave the money to those overseeing the work on the LORD's house. They hired stonecutters and carpenters to restore it, as well as workers in iron and bronze to repair it.|Retains trades and the distinction between funding supervisors and workers.

24:13|The workers went about their tasks, and under their hands the repairs progressed. They restored God's house to its proper condition and made it strong.|Carries the healing/repair image naturally without inventing architectural specifications.

24:14|When they finished, they brought the remaining money to the king and Jehoiada. It was used to make utensils for the LORD's house: utensils for service and burnt offerings, dishes, and gold and silver vessels. Burnt offerings were offered regularly in the LORD's house throughout Jehoiada's lifetime.|Keeps surplus utensils here despite the Kings parallel, and repeats lifetime limit.
24:15|Jehoiada grew old, full of days, and died. He was one hundred thirty years old when he died.|Retains full-of-days image and exceptional age without correction.
24:16|They buried him in the City of David with the kings, because he had done good in Israel, toward God and his house.|Preserves royal burial's stated reason and prepares contrast with Joash.
24:17|After Jehoiada died, Judah's officials came and bowed before the king. Then the king listened to them.|Keeps the turning point and courtly gesture without guessing motives.

24:18|They abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their ancestors, and served the Asherah poles and idols. Wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem because of this guilt.|Retains corporate apostasy and wrath as the narrative's assessment.
24:19|He sent prophets among them to bring them back to the LORD. The prophets warned them, but they would not listen.|Keeps repeated refusal and purpose of prophetic sending.

24:20|Then God's Spirit clothed Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest. He stood above the people and told them, “This is what God says: Why are you breaking the LORD's commands? You will not prosper. Because you have abandoned the LORD, he has abandoned you.”|Preserves clothing image and the mirrored abandonment rather than smoothing its force.
24:21|They conspired against him and, at the king's command, stoned him in the court of the LORD's house.|Names royal responsibility and sacred location of the killing.

24:22|King Joash did not remember the loyal love that Jehoiada, Zechariah's father, had shown him. Yet he killed Jehoiada's son. As Zechariah was dying, he said, “May the LORD see and call you to account!”|Clarifies fathers and sons while retaining remember, loyal love, and dying appeal.

24:23|At the turn of the year, the Aramean army marched against Joash. They entered Judah and Jerusalem, destroyed all the people's officials, and sent all their plunder to the king of Damascus.|Retains seasonal phrasing and all officials without limiting destruction to defeat.

24:24|The Aramean army came with few men, yet the LORD handed over a very large army to them because Judah had abandoned the LORD, the God of their ancestors. They executed judgment on Joash.|Preserves unequal numbers and narrative judgment without claiming Aramean moral superiority.

24:25|When they withdrew, they left him gravely wounded. His servants conspired against him because of the blood of Jehoiada the priest's sons. They killed him on his bed, and he died. They buried him in the City of David, but not in the royal tombs.|Retains plural sons in the Hebrew and burial exclusion; notes singular contextual difficulty.

24:26|Those who conspired against him were Zabad son of Shimeath the Ammonite woman and Jehozabad son of Shimrith the Moabite woman.|Preserves both maternal names, genders, and ethnic identifications without added inference.

24:27|The account of his sons, the many pronouncements against him, and the rebuilding of God's house is written in the exposition of the Book of the Kings. His son Amaziah succeeded him as king.|Renders difficult increased-burden phrase as many pronouncements with alternative noted.
25:1|Amaziah was twenty-five when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother's name was Jehoaddan, from Jerusalem.|Preserves both royal figures and the maternal name.
25:2|He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, but not with an undivided heart.|Keeps the inner qualification central to the ensuing reign.
25:3|Once his hold on the kingdom was secure, he killed the servants who had struck down his father the king.|Links consolidation to punishment without implying a new murder conspiracy.

25:4|But he did not put their sons to death, following what is written in the law, in the book of Moses, where the LORD commanded: “Fathers must not die for their children, and children must not die for their fathers. Each must die for his own sin.”|Retains specific sons and the quoted principle of individual liability.

25:5|Amaziah assembled Judah and arranged all Judah and Benjamin by ancestral families under commanders of thousands and hundreds. He mustered the men twenty years old and upward and found three hundred thousand selected men fit for military service, able to handle spear and large shield.|Preserves age threshold, total, tribal scope, and two command levels.
25:6|He also hired one hundred thousand capable warriors from Israel for one hundred talents of silver.|Keeps troop number, payment, and ancient weight unit distinct.

25:7|But a man of God came to him and said, “King, do not let Israel's army go with you. The LORD is not with Israel—with any of the Ephraimites.|Retains the emphatic exclusion and the prophet's address without universalizing beyond the speech.

25:8|Go, then! Act! Be strong for battle! God will make you stumble before the enemy, for God has power both to help and to make people stumble.”|Preserves abrupt imperatives and ensuing warning; notes disputed conditional force.

25:9|Amaziah asked the man of God, “What about the hundred talents I gave Israel's troops?” The man of God answered, “The LORD can give you much more than that.”|Maintains money question and direct answer, without turning it into a general prosperity promise.

25:10|So Amaziah dismissed the troops who had come to him from Ephraim and sent them home. They became furious with Judah and went home burning with anger.|Keeps both anger descriptions and their target Judah.
25:11|Amaziah gathered his courage, led his people to the Valley of Salt, and struck down ten thousand men of Seir.|Preserves named valley, Seir identity, and casualty figure.

25:12|The men of Judah captured another ten thousand alive. They brought them to the top of a cliff and threw them down from it, and every one of them was torn apart.|Retains atrocity against living prisoners and bodily outcome without euphemism.

25:13|Meanwhile, the troops Amaziah had sent back from going with him to battle raided Judah's cities, from Samaria to Beth-horon. They struck down three thousand people and took a great deal of plunder.|Retains difficult geographical span rather than silently substituting another city.

25:14|After Amaziah returned from striking down the Edomites, he brought the gods of the people of Seir and set them up as his own gods. He bowed before them and burned offerings to them.|Keeps the narrative irony of adopting the defeated people's gods.

25:15|The LORD's anger burned against Amaziah. He sent him a prophet, who said, “Why have you sought the gods of a people whose gods could not rescue them from your hand?”|Preserves seeking vocabulary and the prophet's pointed inability argument.

25:16|While the prophet was speaking, the king interrupted him: “Have we made you a royal adviser? Stop! Why should you be struck down?” The prophet stopped, but said, “I know God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my advice.”|Keeps threat and repeated counsel language in the exchange.

25:17|After taking counsel, Amaziah king of Judah sent this message to Joash son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel: “Come, let us face each other!”|Retains battle challenge's face image and identifies the other Joash by lineage.

25:18|Joash king of Israel sent word back to Amaziah king of Judah: “A thistle in Lebanon sent a message to a cedar in Lebanon: ‘Give your daughter to my son as a wife.’ But a wild animal in Lebanon passed by and trampled the thistle.|Preserves fable's plants, animal, marriage proposal, and repeated Lebanon.

25:19|You say, ‘Look, I have defeated Edom!’ Your heart has lifted you up to seek glory. Stay home now. Why provoke disaster and bring yourself down, and Judah with you?”|Keeps inflated-heart image and warning of shared national consequences.

25:20|Amaziah would not listen. This came from God, so that they would be handed over, because they had sought Edom's gods.|Retains divine causation and plural responsibility without specifying an absent recipient.
25:21|So Joash king of Israel marched up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced each other at Beth-shemesh in Judah.|Echoes face-to-face challenge and identifies the battlefield.
25:22|Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled to his own tent.|Keeps tent image rather than erasing the flight formula.

25:23|At Beth-shemesh, Joash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, son of Joash, son of Jehoahaz. He brought him to Jerusalem and broke down four hundred cubits of its wall, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.|Retains Jehoahaz lineage, captive movement, gates, and four hundred cubits.

25:24|He took all the gold and silver, all the utensils found in God's house under Obed-edom's care, the palace treasures, and hostages. Then he returned to Samaria.|Supplies took for the Hebrew verbless inventory; retains human hostages alongside property.
25:25|Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Joash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel.|Keeps both similarly named dynasties clear and the fifteen-year interval.
25:26|The rest of Amaziah's acts, from first to last, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.|Preserves documentary attribution without implying the modern book's exact identity.

25:27|From the time Amaziah turned away from following the LORD, a conspiracy formed against him in Jerusalem. He fled to Lachish, but they sent men after him there and killed him.|Retains turning-away link and pursuit without inventing conspirators' identities.
25:28|They brought him back on horses and buried him with his ancestors in the city of Judah.|Retains pinned city of Judah rather than silently harmonizing to City of David.

26:1|All the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.|Preserves popular installation and age without assigning an unstated accession date.
26:2|He rebuilt Eloth and restored it to Judah after the king rested with his ancestors.|Retains temporal reference to the preceding king and Eloth's restoration.

26:3|Uzziah was sixteen when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for fifty-two years. His mother's name was Jecoliah, from Jerusalem.|Follows read maternal name and preserves repeated age and long reign.
26:4|He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, following all that his father Amaziah had done.|Keeps the qualified paternal model without rewriting the preceding account.

26:5|He sought God during the lifetime of Zechariah, who understood visions of God. As long as he sought the LORD, God gave him success.|Retains visions reading and the conditional link between seeking and success.

26:6|He went out to war against the Philistines and broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod. He built cities in the Ashdod region and elsewhere among the Philistines.|Preserves three cities and distinguishes destruction from subsequent construction.
26:7|God helped him against the Philistines, the Arabs living in Gur-baal, and the Meunites.|Follows read Arabs and retains three distinct opponents and divine help.

26:8|The Ammonites paid tribute to Uzziah. His reputation reached as far as the entrance to Egypt, for he had become extraordinarily strong.|Preserves Ammonites rather than harmonizing them to adjacent Meunites.
26:9|Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate, and the angle of the wall, and fortified them.|Keeps three construction sites without overidentifying the wall's angle.

26:10|He built towers in the wilderness and cut many cisterns, because he had large herds, both in the foothills and on the plain. He had farmers and vinedressers in the hills and fertile fields, for he loved the soil.|Preserves agriculture, terrain, and affection for the soil as more than military policy.

26:11|Uzziah had an army ready for war, going out in divisions according to the muster prepared by Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the officer, under Hananiah, one of the king's commanders.|Follows read Jeiel and retains the chain of administrative command.
26:12|The total number of ancestral family heads among the capable warriors was two thousand six hundred.|Distinguishes leaders' count from the following troop total.

26:13|Under them was an army of three hundred seven thousand five hundred men, a powerful fighting force to help the king against the enemy.|Preserves precise total and the army's stated supporting purpose.
26:14|Uzziah supplied the whole army with shields, spears, helmets, armor, bows, and slingstones.|Keeps all six equipment categories without specifying modern armor types.

26:15|In Jerusalem he made devices designed by skilled men for the towers and corners, to shoot arrows and large stones. His reputation spread far, for he was wonderfully helped until he became strong.|Keeps devices unspecific and preserves helped/strong transition into the next verse.

26:16|But once he became strong, his heart grew proud, to his ruin. He was unfaithful to the LORD his God and entered the LORD's temple to burn incense on the incense altar.|Preserves strength-pride-ruin sequence and identifies the precise sacred intrusion.
26:17|Azariah the priest went in after him with eighty courageous priests of the LORD.|Keeps eighty and their courage rather than military status.

26:18|They confronted King Uzziah: “It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD. That belongs to the priests, Aaron's descendants, who are consecrated to burn incense. Leave the sanctuary! You have been unfaithful, and the LORD God will not honor you for this.”|Preserves Aaronic restriction and confrontation without generalizing it into political doctrine.

26:19|Uzziah became furious. He had a censer in his hand to burn incense, and while he raged at the priests, a skin disease broke out on his forehead before them in the LORD's house, beside the incense altar.|Retains bodily sign, timing, and location without diagnosing modern Hansen's disease.

26:20|Azariah the chief priest and all the priests turned toward him and saw the disease on his forehead. They hurried him out. He himself rushed to leave, because the LORD had struck him.|Distinguishes priests' removal and Uzziah's own haste with divine attribution intact.

26:21|King Uzziah had the skin disease until the day he died. He lived in a separate house because of it, cut off from the LORD's house. His son Jotham was in charge of the palace and governed the people of the land.|Preserves lasting exclusion and separate administration, with house terminology noted.
26:22|Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet wrote the rest of Uzziah's acts, from first to last.|Keeps named prophetic writer without claiming identity with canonical Isaiah passages.

26:23|Uzziah rested with his ancestors. They buried him beside them in the burial field belonging to the kings, for they said, “He had the skin disease.” His son Jotham succeeded him as king.|Distinguishes burial field from royal tombs and retains stated rationale.

27:1|Jotham was twenty-five when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. His mother's name was Jerushah daughter of Zadok.|Preserves age, reign length, maternal name, and maternal grandfather.

27:2|He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, following all that his father Uzziah had done, except that he did not enter the LORD's temple. The people, however, continued their corrupt ways.|Keeps the crucial exception and separate assessment of the people.
27:3|He built the Upper Gate of the LORD's house and did extensive building on the wall of the Ophel.|Retains Ophel as a named location with vocabulary support.
27:4|He built cities in Judah's hill country, and fortresses and towers in the wooded regions.|Preserves two terrain zones and different fortifications.

27:5|He fought the king of the Ammonites and prevailed over them. That year the Ammonites gave him one hundred talents of silver, ten thousand kors of wheat, and ten thousand of barley. They paid him the same in the second and third years.|Keeps three annual payments and distinct weight and grain units.
27:6|Jotham grew strong because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God.|Retains prepared ways before God as sustained direction rather than a single act.
27:7|The rest of Jotham's acts, all his wars, and his ways are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.|Preserves wars and ways as separate documentary categories.
27:8|He was twenty-five when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years.|Retains deliberate repetition of both royal figures.
27:9|Jotham rested with his ancestors and was buried in the City of David. His son Ahaz succeeded him as king.|Keeps burial and succession formula in clear narrative sequence.

28:1|Ahaz was twenty when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. Unlike his ancestor David, he did not do what was right in the LORD's eyes.|Preserves figures and Davidic comparison without conflating father and ancestor.
28:2|He followed the ways of Israel's kings and even made cast images for the Baals.|Retains metal-cast objects and plural Baals.

28:3|He burned offerings in the Valley of Ben-hinnom and burned his sons in the fire, following the detestable practices of the nations the LORD had driven out before Israel.|Keeps sons plural and burning explicit, not a harmless passage-through-fire euphemism.
